exercises.intro: This set of texts is about a city tree program. Section A is a public notice. Section B is an information box. Section C is a news article.
exercises.context:
Section A:
Riverside Park Tree Adoption Day
Saturday, May 9, 9:00 a.m. – 1:00 p.m.

Help us plant 200 native trees along the river! No experience is necessary — our staff will provide tools, gloves, and instruction. Volunteers under 16 must be accompanied by an adult. Lunch will be provided for all registered volunteers. Space is limited to 80 participants, so register online by May 2 at the Parks Department website. Rain date: May 16.

Section B:
Did you know?

A single mature tree can absorb about 20 kilograms of carbon dioxide per year and release enough oxygen for two people. Trees planted on the west side of a house can reduce summer air-conditioning costs by up to 30 percent. Studies have also shown that shoppers spend more time — and more money — in tree-lined shopping districts, and that houses on streets with trees sell faster and at higher prices than similar houses on treeless streets.

Section C:
When Riverdale launched its "20,000 Trees" campaign five years ago, skeptics called it a publicity stunt. The city promised to plant 20,000 trees in five years — a number that seemed designed for headlines rather than for reality. This spring, however, the city announced that it had planted its 21,000th tree, exceeding its goal with months to spare.

The program's success rests on an unusual strategy: rather than doing all the work itself, the city gives trees away. Residents who agree to plant and water a tree in their yard receive one free of charge, along with instructions and a follow-up visit from a city arborist. Schools and businesses can request larger plantings, which the city installs with the help of volunteers. According to program director Ana Costa, the approach works because it spreads responsibility. "A city crew can plant a tree in an hour," she says, "but that tree needs water every week for three years. We can't be everywhere — so we recruit the neighborhood."

Not everyone is convinced. A recent audit found that about 15 percent of the trees planted in the campaign's first two years have died, most of them from lack of water during a drought. City officials acknowledge the losses but note that survival rates have improved since the city began requiring adopters to attend a short training session. "We learned that handing someone a tree is the easy part," Costa admits. "Teaching them to keep it alive is the real program."
exercises.question: The following question refers to all three sections. Which statement would program director Ana Costa most likely agree with?
options: Tree planting should be left to professional city crews.
A campaign succeeds through long-term community care, not just planting.
Publicity is more important than survival rates.
Trees grow best along rivers and in parks.
exercises.explanation: Costa's final quote — 'Teaching them to keep it alive is the real program' — shows she values ongoing care over the planting event itself. A is the opposite of her strategy.

exercises.intro: This passage is about trees in cities.
exercises.context:
City trees do far more than decorate sidewalks. A mature tree can intercept thousands of liters of rainwater each year, easing pressure on storm drains during heavy rains. Its leaves filter dust and pollutants from the air, and its shade can lower the temperature of a street by several degrees — a benefit of growing importance as cities experience more frequent heat waves. Researchers have even found that hospital patients recover faster when their windows look out on trees.

Yet the life of a city tree is remarkably hard. Roots are squeezed into small pits of compacted soil, often surrounded by pavement that blocks water and air. Road salt, car exhaust, and construction damage add to the stress. As a result, the average street tree in a dense city center may live only a fraction of the lifespan it would enjoy in a forest.

The benefits of urban trees are also distributed unevenly. Wealthier neighborhoods tend to have far more tree cover than poorer ones, a pattern documented in cities around the world. Because trees lower temperatures and improve air quality, this inequality has real consequences for public health, particularly during heat waves.

In response, many cities have launched ambitious planting campaigns. Some now map every street tree and measure the "canopy cover" of each neighborhood, directing new plantings toward the areas that need them most. Experts caution, however, that planting is only the beginning: a young tree requires years of watering and care before it can survive on its own, and campaigns that count saplings planted but not trees surviving often achieve less than they promise.
exercises.question: Why does the author mention wealthier neighborhoods?
options: to show where the oldest trees are found
to suggest that trees increase property values
to show that tree cover is unequal within cities
to explain where planting campaigns began
exercises.explanation: The topic sentence of paragraph 3 is that benefits are 'distributed unevenly'; the comparison between wealthy and poor neighborhoods illustrates exactly that point.

Saturday, May 9, 9:00 a.m. – 1:00 p.m.

Help us plant 200 native trees along the river! No experience is necessary — our staff will provide tools, gloves, and instruction. Volunteers under 16 must be accompanied by an adult. Lunch will be provided for all registered volunteers. Space is limited to 80 participants, so register online by May 2 at the Parks Department website. Rain date: May 16.

Section B:
Did you know?

A single mature tree can absorb about 20 kilograms of carbon dioxide per year and release enough oxygen for two people. Trees planted on the west side of a house can reduce summer air-conditioning costs by up to 30 percent. Studies have also shown that shoppers spend more time — and more money — in tree-lined shopping districts, and that houses on streets with trees sell faster and at higher prices than similar houses on treeless streets.

Section C:
When Riverdale launched its "20,000 Trees" campaign five years ago, skeptics called it a publicity stunt. The city promised to plant 20,000 trees in five years — a number that seemed designed for headlines rather than for reality. This spring, however, the city announced that it had planted its 21,000th tree, exceeding its goal with months to spare.

The program's success rests on an unusual strategy: rather than doing all the work itself, the city gives trees away. Residents who agree to plant and water a tree in their yard receive one free of charge, along with instructions and a follow-up visit from a city arborist. Schools and businesses can request larger plantings, which the city installs with the help of volunteers. According to program director Ana Costa, the approach works because it spreads responsibility. "A city crew can plant a tree in an hour," she says, "but that tree needs water every week for three years. We can't be everywhere — so we recruit the neighborhood."

Not everyone is convinced. A recent audit found that about 15 percent of the trees planted in the campaign's first two years have died, most of them from lack of water during a drought. City officials acknowledge the losses but note that survival rates have improved since the city began requiring adopters to attend a short training session. "We learned that handing someone a tree is the easy part," Costa admits. "Teaching them to keep it alive is the real program."
